title_guess: Banking sector reforms after 1991: the Committee on Financial System (Narasimham) recommendations on bank consolidation, new private banks, less government ownership, and regulation and supervision, with how each was implemented
recurring_cast: committee_desk (five dark figures, the chair in red, 'Committee on Financial System' plate) with a 'Narasimhan' name and a recommendations document

horizontal policy timeline with a flag at 1947, NATIONALIZATION in blue, a law icon at 1980 and a red ECONOMIC CRISIS / PROBLEMS bar
bank_building icons (small grid, big stacks, a single 'public sector bank')
Private players ← sell ← % ← public sector bank hook line
brand_logo (RBI emblem coin) and the Ministry of Finance banking-division logo
number chips 1-4 under the framed agenda box counting sub-recommendations
running_examples: bank mergers by year: 1993 New Bank of India → PNB (and United Bank of India → Allahabad Bank, doubtful), 2004 Global Trust Bank → OBC, 2008 State Bank of Saurashtra → SBI, 2010 State Bank of Indore → SBI, 2017 remaining SBI associates → SBI, 2019 ten PSBs → four
2019 merger table: OBC + United Bank of India → PNB; Andhra + Corporation → Union Bank of India; Syndicate → Canara; Allahabad → Indian Bank; 12 PSBs left
new private banks with founding years: UTI/Axis 1993, HDFC, ICICI, IndusInd 1994, Kotak 2003, Yes 2004, Bandhan 2014, IDFC First 2015

segments.teaches: recall: banks were nationalised up to 1980; an economic crisis followed in the late 1980s; in 1991 the Committee on Financial System (CFS) was set up and its recommendations for the financial sector included banking sector reforms

elements.what: blue line from a flag at 1947 (NATIONALIZATION) to 1980, red ECONOMIC CRISIS stretch to 1991, blue after 1991
'Banking sector was 100% nationalised' on a stem at 1980
committee table of five figures, chair in red, plate 'Committee on Financial System', fed by a red elbow arrow from 1991
'Narasimhan' name with a dotted line to a recommendations document with a tick
recommendations → financial sector reforms → dotted arrow back down to 'BANKING SECTOR REFORMS' after 1991

segments.notes: 7 change events in 40 s (~every 6 s). Doubtful facts to verify: '100% nationalised' (the video itself says 85% at 629 s) and nationalisation starting at 1947. The chair's name is shown, not spoken.
segments.idea: the 1991 crisis brought a committee whose advice reshaped banking
segments.shown_as: a policy timeline draws from a flag at 1947 through a blue NATIONALIZATION stretch to a 1980 stem marked '100% nationalised', then a red ECONOMIC CRISIS stretch to 1991; from 1991 a red elbow rises to a committee table with a red chair; a recommendations document, 'financial sector reforms' and a dotted arrow lead back down to 'banking sector reforms' on the timeline

segments.teaches: the banking recommendations fall under four headings; after 1991 the government made a complete U-turn from nationalisation to privatisation

elements.what: four grey boxes under 'Banking sector reforms': bank consolidation, entry of new private banks, reduction in government ownership, bank regulation and supervision
red-ringed U-turn road sign under the NATIONALIZATION stretch, later a plain black U-turn arrow
'PRIVATIZATION' spaced capitals under the four boxes

segments.notes: 10 change events in 31 s. The four boxes write on during an 8 s transcript gap (38.9-47.3 s), so what was said over them is unknown. The U-turn sign is a strong one-glance picture of a policy reversal.
segments.idea: four reform headings, all pointing away from state ownership
segments.shown_as: four grey boxes write on one by one under 'banking sector reforms'; a red-ringed U-turn sign pops onto the NATIONALIZATION stretch of the timeline and pulses as 'U-turn' is said, then becomes a plain black U-turn arrow while 'PRIVATIZATION' writes under the list

segments.teaches: bank consolidation: India has many small banks; banks with similar business models should merge into fewer large banks, which have a bigger capital base, lower operating cost and wider reach, so they are financially strong enough to compete with international banks

elements.what: committee, recommendations and the four boxes moved into a left panel; 'Bank consolidation' framed in black
grid of 24 small bank icons labelled 'large number of small banks'
top note: CFS suggested merging banks with similar business models into larger entities
the grid collapses into four tall stacks of bank icons
label struck and rewritten: 'small number of large banks'
gold medallion with a bank inside, tagged 'Large entities' then '[Financially strong]'
increased capital base, reduced operation cost, increased market reach
box: can compete more effectively with international banks

segments.notes: 11 change events in 57 s (~every 5 s). The grid-to-stacks merge plus the struck label is the best picture in the video. Saancha: left agenda panel with the current box framed stays for the rest of the video.
segments.idea: merge many small banks into a few big ones, and the big ones are stronger
segments.shown_as: the timeline clears and the committee slides into a left agenda panel with 'bank consolidation' framed; at right a grid of 24 small bank icons appears over 'large number of small banks'; the grid collapses into four tall stacks as the label is struck to 'small number of large banks'; a gold medallion bank labelled 'large entities' grows three benefit bullets, a 'financially strong' tag and a line up to 'can compete with international banks'

each row: bank name ...... 'Merged' → bigger bank

segments.teaches: the 2019 mega-merger: OBC and United Bank of India into PNB, Andhra Bank and Corporation Bank into Union Bank of India, Syndicate Bank into Canara Bank, Allahabad Bank into Indian Bank; now only 12 public sector banks remain

segments.teaches: entry of new private banks, background: by the 1980s banks were nationalised, but most nationalised banks were loss-making, inefficient, with rising non-performing assets

elements.what: 1947 flag → NATIONALIZATION → law icon at 1980 with '100% nationalised' stem
red bar 'PROBLEMS WITH THE NATIONALISED BANKS' running on after 1980
'Nationalised banks suffered a set of problems': lack of profitability, inefficiency, high levels of NPAs

segments.notes: 6 change events in 30 s (~every 5 s). The red problem bar continuing the blue nationalisation line ties the problems to that policy. '100%' repeated (doubtful).
segments.idea: nationalised banks ended up unprofitable and inefficient
segments.shown_as: the agenda frame moves to 'entry of new private banks'; at right the nationalisation timeline redraws to a law icon at 1980, and a red 'problems with the nationalised banks' bar runs on from it; three problem bullets write on under it

segments.teaches: why: the government kept directing nationalised banks to lend to farming, small industry and priority sectors at concessional rates for populist reasons, so profit was impossible; and with all banks alike there was no competition, hence no push to improve

elements.what: big '? WHY' with an elbow arrow up from the red problem bar
brace beside WHY: directed and concessional lending for populist reasons; lack of competition

segments.notes: 3 change events in 56 s (~every 19 s); long voice-led stretch. Spoken but not shown: the sectors (agriculture, small-scale industry, priority sectors) and the 'social welfare work' framing.
segments.idea: forced cheap lending and no competition caused the losses
segments.shown_as: the timeline drops away; the red problem bar and its bullets move up and an elbow arrow rises to a big '? WHY'; a brace opens beside it and two reasons write on: directed concessional lending, then lack of competition

segments.teaches: CFS recommended letting new private banks in, to create competition and push all banks to be efficient; but private banks may take too much risk for profit and a failure can trigger a crisis, so the committee also asked for strict regulation

elements.what: blue paragraph: new private banks should be allowed in to raise competition and efficiency
yellow alarm bell swinging above the paragraph
second paragraph under a line: CFS asked for strict regulatory requirements on these private banks

segments.notes: 3 change events in 67 s: a text-only stretch with a decorative bell for 'khatre ki ghanti'. The risk story (high risk for profit, a failed bank triggering a crisis) is spoken only; a falling bank with a crack spreading to others would show it.
segments.idea: private banks bring competition but also risk, so they need strict rules
segments.shown_as: the right side clears to a blue paragraph about letting private banks in; a yellow bell drops in and swings for about half a minute as the danger is described; a second paragraph about strict regulation writes on under a line

segments.teaches: implementation: the first new private bank, UTI Bank, opened in 1993 (renamed Axis Bank in 2007); then HDFC, ICICI and IndusInd in 1994, Kotak Mahindra 2003, Yes 2004, Bandhan 2014, IDFC 2015

BIE should not copy real bank names as a picture; a timeline of generic new bank icons opening their doors would carry it.
segments.idea: new private banks opened from 1993 onward
segments.shown_as: the paragraph slides up and a grey two-column table of eight private banks with founding years appears at once and stays while the years are read

segments.teaches: reduction in government ownership: the government may sell part of its stake in public sector banks on the capital market; this brings fresh capital, and private owners bring managerial professionalism

segments.idea: selling a slice of a state bank brings money and private management skills

segments.teaches: the SBI (Amendment) Act 1993 let SBI sell shares on the capital market up to 33% (as stated); today the government holds 57.49% of SBI, mutual funds 13.2%, other domestic institutions 12.16%, foreign institutions 10.09%, the public about 7%; the Banking Companies (Amendment) Act 1994 let nationalised banks sell up to 33%

segments.teaches: so far the government could sell up to 33%; but its 1999 disinvestment policy said it would sell even a majority stake (over 50%) to a strategic partner with banking experience; whoever holds the majority owns the bank, so this is privatisation of banks; no such step has been taken yet (as stated)

segments.teaches: regulation and supervision: before 1969 private banks dominated; the 1969 nationalisation act made 85% of banking public; the government wanted control, so a banking division under the Ministry of Finance got operational control while RBI kept regulation and supervision: dual control; CFS said end dual control at once and make RBI the sole regulator
